title: Sarkhej Roza

photos.alt: The Sarkhej Roza mosque seen across its wide stone-paved courtyard: a long arcaded building with a row of small domes and one large central dome.
photos.caption: Sarkhej Roza, front view across the courtyard (photographed 2011).
photos.author: Museeb fakih

facts.text: A complex of tombs and a mosque in Makarba, about 7 km south-west of central Ahmedabad.
The tomb was begun in 1445 under Muhammad Shah II and completed in 1451 under his son Qutbuddin Ahmad Shah II.
Sultan Mahmud Begada later expanded the complex greatly, adding a palace and a mausoleum for himself and his family.
It is a Monument of National Importance on the Archaeological Survey of India's list; encroachment has reduced the complex from about 29 to about 14 hectares.
Le Corbusier compared its design to the Acropolis of Athens, which is why it is sometimes called the "Acropolis of Ahmedabad".

why: It is the historic anchor of the area and a nationally protected monument, so it is the natural reference point for the streets, stalls and transport around it.

title: Shaikh Ahmed Khattu Ganj Bakhsh

facts.text: The tomb at the heart of the Roza was built in honour of the Sufi saint Shaikh Ahmed Khattu Ganj Bakhsh, who died at Sarkhej in 1445.
His mausoleum is described as the largest of its kind in Gujarat.

why: The saint's tomb is the reason the Roza was built, and it remains the heart of the complex that the rest of the area grew around.

title: Sarkhej Lake

photos.alt: Sepia albumen print of a carved stone wall with three round openings, the outlet of the Sarkhej tank, with a large tree behind it.
photos.caption: Outlet of the Sarkhej tank, photographed in 1855 by William Johnson.
photos.author: William Johnson (photographer); SMU Central University Libraries

photos.alt: Engraving of a two-storey colonnaded gallery with steps down to the water, an elephant at the left and small boats in front.
photos.caption: Engraving of the gallery leading to the queens' tombs at Sarkhej, from Louis Rousselet's book on India (1878).
photos.author: Louis Rousselet

facts.text: A lake of about 6.9 hectares was dug under Mahmud Begada and surrounded with cut stone steps.
Mahmud Begada built a palace, now in ruins, at the lake's south-west corner.

why: Water and stepped edges make the lake the complex's open public space, and it ties the monuments together.

title: Ahmed Shah I and Ahmedabad

facts.text: Ahmed Shah I laid the foundation of Ahmedabad on 26 February 1411 and named the city after himself.

why: Sarkhej's monuments belong to the same Sultanate period that founded the city, which links this edge of Ahmedabad to its origins.

title: Sarkhej–Gandhinagar Highway

photos.alt: A wide divided highway with light traffic, street lamps along the median and apartment blocks and power pylons on the left.
photos.caption: Sarkhej–Gandhinagar Highway, Ahmedabad (photographed 2012).
photos.author: Abhishek.ujoshi

facts.text: A highway of about 44.5 km running from Sarkhej in the south-west to Gandhinagar in the north.
It forms a major part of National Highway 147; in 2015 its administration passed from the NHAI to the Government of Gujarat.

why: It is the area's main link to the rest of the city, bringing buses, autos and visitors, and with them traffic pressure at the junctions.

title: Makarba

facts.text: Recorded as a census town in Ahmedabad district, with a population of 18,090 at the 2001 census.

why: It is the setting for everything on this map: the Roza, the lake and the places and stories are all in and around Makarba.

title: Ahmedabad's textile mills (city-wide context)

photos.alt: A tall brick mill chimney rising above trees, with the dome of a small stone mosque in the foreground.
photos.caption: The Calico Mills chimney in Ahmedabad, with Baba Lului's Mosque in front (photographed 2021). Not in Makarba.
photos.author: Imfarhad7

facts.text: Its textile industry earned Ahmedabad the nickname "Manchester of India".
From the mid-1970s, facing competition from automation and specialised domestic looms, several mills closed, leaving tens of thousands of workers without income.

why: City-wide context: mill closures are part of how Ahmedabad's working neighbourhoods changed.
